metadata.title: Count Prime Powers, Not Huge Numbers
metadata.description: Count prime factors with multiplicity, highest powers in factorials, and trailing zeros in structured products.

content.text: Prime factorization turns enormous products into exponent bookkeeping. If a base is itself composite, expand it first—for example, 30^7 contributes 2^7×3^7.
For the highest power of p in n!, use Legendre's sum floor(n/p)+floor(n/p²)+... . For trailing zeros, count pairs of 2 and 5; usually 5 is the limiting factor.
Let's find the highest power of 9 in 99!.
In products of even numbers, repeated 2s are abundant. In products of odd numbers, there may be many 5s but no 2s. Always identify which prime is limiting before counting.
Now count zeros in a product built from multiples of 10.
Finish with the product of all even numbers through 100.
Excellent. Large products are now exponent-counting exercises instead of multiplication exercises.
